title: Energy Resources and Energy Transfers
blurb: Smaller than the first three chapters, but very predictable: specific heat capacity (definition, calculation and experiment) plus one discussion question on generating electricity.
formulas: mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change
useful energy output ÷ total energy input (× 100%)

items.q: State what is meant by the term specific heat capacity.
items.rx: meant by the term specific heat capacity
a: The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance
by 1 °C (or 1 K).
items.tip: You must have all three parts: the energy, the 1 kg, and the 1 degree. Missing the mass loses the mark.

items.q: Use the student's results to calculate the specific heat capacity of the water / liquid.
a: Find the energy supplied, e.g. E = I × V × t (or read it from the joulemeter);
use the rearranged formula c = energy ÷ (mass × temperature change);
substitute with mass in kg and the temperature change (not the final temperature);
evaluate and give the unit J/(kg °C).
items.tip: Δθ is the change in temperature. Subtract the start from the finish - do not use the final reading on its own.

items.q: Describe an investigation to determine the specific heat capacity of water.
a: Measure the mass of the water with a balance (weigh the beaker empty, then with water, and subtract);
record the starting temperature with a thermometer;
heat with an electrical immersion heater for a measured time using a stopwatch;
measure the current and voltage with an ammeter and voltmeter, so energy = I × V × t;
record the final (highest) temperature and find the temperature change;
calculate c = energy ÷ (mass × temperature change);
insulate the container and use a lid to reduce heat loss to the surroundings.
items.tip: The improvement mark is almost always about insulation or lagging. The main systematic error is energy lost to the surroundings, which makes the measured value too high.

items.q: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of generating electricity using solar panels / solar farms.
a: Advantages: renewable and will not run out; no carbon dioxide or other polluting gases released while generating; low running costs; useful in remote locations with no grid connection;

Disadvantages: high initial installation cost; output depends on the weather and the time of day, and is zero at night; needs a very large area of land for the power produced; energy cannot easily be stored for later use.
items.tip: Balance the answer - give both sides. Naming a specific comparison with fossil fuels or another named source usually picks up the last mark.

items.q: Describe the energy transfers taking place.
a: Name the store the energy starts in and the store it ends in (chemical, kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic, thermal, nuclear);
name the pathway: mechanically (by a force), electrically, by heating, or by radiation;
state that energy is conserved - the total stays the same, but some is dissipated to the surroundings as thermal energy.
items.tip: Use the word 'store' and the word 'transferred'. Never say energy is 'used up', 'lost' or 'created'.

items.q: Calculate the efficiency of the device.
a: efficiency = useful energy (or power) output ÷ total energy (or power) input;
multiply by 100 if a percentage is asked for;
the answer must be less than 1 (or less than 100%).
items.tip: Wasted energy = total input − useful output. If your efficiency comes out above 100%, you have the fraction upside down.

items.q: Explain how thermal energy is transferred by conduction, convection and radiation, and how the transfer can be reduced.
a: Conduction: particles vibrate more and pass energy to neighbouring particles; in metals free electrons carry energy quickly, which is why metals are good conductors;
Convection: heated fluid expands and becomes less dense, so it rises, and cooler denser fluid sinks to replace it, forming a convection current;
Radiation: energy transferred as infrared electromagnetic waves and needs no medium; dull black surfaces are the best emitters and absorbers, shiny silver surfaces the worst;
To reduce transfer: use insulation and trapped air (a poor conductor), shiny reflective surfaces, and a vacuum to stop conduction and convection.
items.tip: Convection needs the words 'less dense' and 'rises'. Saying 'heat rises' on its own scores nothing.

items.q: Use conservation of energy to find the speed of a falling object (GPE to KE).
a: GPE lost = mass × g × height;
assume all of this is transferred to the kinetic energy store: ½ × m × v² = m × g × h;
rearrange for v and evaluate;
in reality some energy is transferred to thermal energy by air resistance, so the real speed is lower.

items.q: Compare renewable and non-renewable energy resources.
a: Non-renewable (coal, oil, gas, nuclear fuel) will run out; they are reliable and give a large, controllable output on demand;
fossil fuels release carbon dioxide, causing the enhanced greenhouse effect, and sulfur dioxide, causing acid rain;
renewables (wind, solar, hydroelectric, tidal, wave, geothermal, biomass) will not run out and release no CO₂ while generating;
but most renewables are unreliable, depending on the weather, the time of day or the tides, and have high set-up costs.
